famous_note: Chapter VII was reprinted separately by Theodor Bibliander, Basel 1543 and 1550, under the title 'Commentatiuncula Savonarolae Mahumeticam sectam omni ratione carere ostendens' (stated in Procter's introduction, read; the 1550 title page read in the Paderborn copy). I did not verify later scholarly citations of this sentence specifically (the HAL article and the Liberty Fund page could not be read).
ref: Girolamo Savonarola, Triumphus crucis, Liber IV, cap. VII (Latin, as reprinted by Bibliander, Basel 1550, 'Mahumetanorum sectam omni ratione carere'; pages 4-5 of the Paderborn excerpt, the passage beginning 'Cur iustis sanctisq;'). English: Procter, The Triumph of the Cross (1901), Book IV, ch. VII, 'The Utter Irrationality of the Mahometan Religion' (Italian-based).
quote_orig: Cur iustis sanctisq; uiris impij & bonorum corruptores, qui plures quàm iusti ad se trahunt, non praeponuntur? O admirabile argumentũ, Mahumetem Christo praeponi, quia rudes & eneruatos populos ipsius fraudibus & pollicitationibus, minis insuper & gladio, à fide Christi sanctissima subductos, ad voluptatem perditosq; mores induxerit.
quote_en: It is indeed a surprising mode of arguing in favour of Mahomet, to say, that he must be superior to Christ, because, by means of the sword, he has subjected many to his irrational and degrading law.
licence_note: English: Procter 1901 (public domain by date); read on Project Gutenberg eBook 74508 (PG licence header read). Latin: 1550 Basel print (public domain by date); the Paderborn PDF's own licence statement was not read.
keys: O admirabile argumentũ, Mahumetem Christo praeponi
what_it_says: Savonarola calls it an 'admirable argument' that Muhammad should be preferred to Christ, because he led simple and enfeebled peoples away from Christ's holy faith by deceits, promises, threats and the sword, toward pleasure and depraved morals.
context: This sentence is part of a passage (Liber IV, cap. VII) in which Savonarola refutes the claim that Islam's success proves its superiority to Christianity; the sentence before asks why, if the number of followers decided truth, the impious should not be preferred to the just. He answers that Christ's teaching was never spread by such means. The Latin is the Bibliander 1550 reprint of the chapter; the English is Procter's rendering of the Italian version.
limits: Procter's English is a translation of Savonarola's Italian version, not of the Latin sentence; the wording differs, the point is the same. The sentence is a rhetorical one-sided argument, not a call to force. It describes the 'promises' and 'sword' as means Muhammad used, which is a historical and doctrinal charge (it is the point of the chapter). Latin read from the page image; 'argumentũ' and 'pollicitationibus' as printed.
stance: own view (the author's own argument, not a quotation of an opponent)

famous_note: Same chapter as sav_01 (Bibliander 1543/1550 reprint; Procter 1901). Later citations not verified.
ref: Savonarola, Triumphus crucis, Liber IV, cap. VII (Latin, Bibliander 1550; pages 2-3 of the Paderborn excerpt, opening of the chapter and the account of Muhammad). English: Procter 1901, Book IV, ch. VII.
quote_orig: Sed haec secta autore gloriatur Mahumete. Qui, sicut certa tradit historia, prorsus irrationabilis, sceleratus, adulter, & populorum praedator fuit. Cumq; epileptico, ut fertur, morbo saepe correptus collaberetur, interrogatus cur id ei contingeret, se angeli colloquio tunc frui referebat. Vi autem & gladio, nõ rationibus instructus, pollicitationibus primũ malaq; arte homines rudes ac impuros sibi asciuit.
quote_en: Mahometanism began with Mahomet, who, as history tells us, was a most unreasonable and unprincipled man, an adulterer, and a robber. He was subject to epileptic fits, which often caused him to fall prostrate, and these falls he attributed to colloquies with an angel. Gradually, and by means, not of argument, but of violence and bribery, he gathered around him a number of uneducated and depraved men; and with their assistance conquered vast multitudes of people.
keys: Sed haec secta autore gloriatur Mahumete
what_it_says: Savonarola says the sect glories in its founder, who by historical report was irrational, wicked, an adulterer and a plunderer of peoples; he had epileptic fits which he took for conversations with an angel, and gathered rude men by violence and bribery.
context: The chapter opens by placing Islam among Jews and heretics, and says the Qur'an is so full of fables and immorality that it deserves ridicule. The founder's character is then used to argue that a bad beginning cannot have a good end. The Latin is the Bibliander 1550 reprint; the English is Procter's rendering of the Italian.
limits: PERSONAL INVECTIVE: 'sceleratus, adulter, & populorum praedator' is a charge against a historical individual, not a call to violence; it is included because the brief lists Muhammad's character as a theme, but the orchestrator should decide whether such personal characterisation is acceptable. The epilepsy story is a late-medieval polemical commonplace; Savonarola gives no source ('ut fertur', 'sicut certa tradit historia'). Procter's English renders the Italian and omits 'ut fertur'. Latin 'nõ' and 'primũ' are printed abbreviations kept as in the page.
stance: own view (author's own characterisation, citing unnamed 'history')

ref: Savonarola, Triumphus crucis, Liber IV, cap. VII (Latin, Bibliander 1550; pages 3-4 of the Paderborn excerpt). English: Procter 1901, Book IV, ch. VII.
quote_orig: Sed inscitiae ac prauitatis suae conscius Mahumetes, callide mandauit, nõ nisi gladio religionẽ suam tuendam esse. Vt quod ratione & honestate defendi non poterat, ferino impetu decerneretur.
quote_en: If Mahomet had attempted to establish his religion by preaching, his errors would have been very easily demonstrated. But, knowing that his doctrine was indefensible on any logical grounds, he had the astuteness to command, that it should be propagated by the sword.
keys: callide mandauit, nõ nisi gladio religionẽ suam tuendam esse
Sed inscitiae ac prauitatis suae conscius Mahumetes
what_it_says: Savonarola says Muhammad, aware that his doctrine could not be defended by reason and honesty, cunningly ordered that his religion be defended only by the sword, so that what could not be argued would be settled by brute force.
context: The sentence comes right after the passage on Muhammad's claim that he was sent to convert by the sword (sav_05). It is Savonarola's explanation of why Islam was spread by arms and not by preaching. The Latin is the Bibliander reprint; the English is Procter's rendering of the Italian.
limits: The point is a historical-doctrinal charge about how the religion spread; it is not a call to wage war, and the next clause ('Cum ... ferino impetu' etc.) is also descriptive. Savonarola attributes the 'sword' policy to Muhammad as a claim; it is his interpretation (the Qur'anic and historical basis is not checked here). The Latin phrase 'nõ nisi' is printed with the abbreviation mark on 'nõ'.

ref: Savonarola, Triumphus crucis, Liber IV, cap. VII (Latin, Bibliander 1550; pages 3-4 of the Paderborn excerpt). English: Procter 1901, Book IV, ch. VII.
quote_orig: Quàm stulte etiam Mahumetes in Alcorano sibimet contradicat, uel ex eo apparet, ubi se nescire fatetur, utrum ipse & sui in via sint salutis, nec ne: neminemq; inter mortales habere, qui Alcoranum intelligat.
quote_en: Mahomet, also, constantly contradicts himself in his Koran. He says that he knows not, whether he and his followers are in the way of salvation; and that he believes, that none can understand his law.
keys: Quàm stulte etiam Mahumetes in Alcorano sibimet contradicat
what_it_says: Savonarola says Muhammad contradicts himself in the Qur'an, admitting he does not know whether he and his followers are saved, and that no mortal understands the Qur'an.
context: This is Savonarola's argument that the Qur'an is self-contradictory and therefore cannot be a divine law. The sentences that follow (not quoted: they contain a rhetorical wish that Muhammad had been stoned) are excluded; see excluded.json.
limits: The 'contradiction' is Savonarola's reading of Qur'anic passages about salvation and understanding (not checked here against the Qur'an; flagged UNVERIFIED as a claim about the text). The quoted sentence ends before 'Nonne is autor ... potius lapidibus obruendus quàm imitandus fuit?'; that next sentence is a call to stone Muhammad and is deliberately excluded from this passage.

ref: Savonarola, Triumphus crucis, Liber IV, cap. VII (Latin, Bibliander 1550; pages 3 of the Paderborn excerpt). English: Procter 1901, Book IV, ch. VII.
quote_orig: Pro certo enim constat, utriusq; Testamenti codices Hebraicis, Graecis, Latinisq; literis iuxta harũ nationum idiomata antiquis monumentis asseruari, & per uniuersum orbem ex ijs complura uolumina eodem exemplo uariis temporibus fideliter esse transcripta, uetustissimisq; nouissima cõfirmari. Quomodo ergo in tot exemplaribus, apud diuersas mundi nationes, uariis linguis, dissimilibusq; hominum studijs & ingeniis potuit hæc simul locũ habere deprauatio? Imò ex huiusmodi scripturarũ consensu illius fabulæ ac mendacia, quibus ineptè procaciterq; utrumq; Testamentũ uitiauit, planè deprehenduntur.
quote_en: Mahomet, in his Koran, approves both the New and the Old Testament. He commends Christ as a true Prophet, born of the Virgin Mary. But, in spite of this, he accuses Christians of having falsified both the Old and the New Testament. Such an accusation will, easily, be rejected by any one who considers the uniformity existing between the versions of the Old and New Testament, whether written in Hebrew, Greek, Latin, or any other language, either ancient or modern. Had Christians tampered with the Scriptures, how could the versions of the Bible be uniform? This would be wonderful, existing, as they do, in so many languages, and written in such numbers of books, both Jewish and Christian, ancient and modern. This very uniformity of all the versions of the Scriptures is a clear proof that the fables of Mahomet, and the Koran itself, are but a tissue of lies.
keys: potuit hæc simul locũ habere deprauatio
what_it_says: Savonarola argues that the uniformity of the Hebrew, Greek and Latin manuscripts of the Old and New Testament across many nations shows that they were not corrupted, so the Qur'anic accusation that Christians falsified Scripture is refuted, and the Qur'an's own fables are exposed.
context: This is Savonarola's answer to the Qur'anic charge of Scriptural falsification (tahrif), which he states as a Muslim claim. The argument is about manuscript uniformity. The English is Procter's rendering; Procter's first sentence ('Mahomet, in his Koran, approves...') is included because it states the Qur'anic claim that is being answered.
limits: The 'accusation' is Savonarola's account of the Muslim position; the Qur'anic text of the charge is not checked here (UNVERIFIED as to the Qur'an). Latin 'hæc simul locũ' is read from the image and may contain a transcription error; the sentence's sense is clear. Procter's English 'the Old and the New Testament' is his rendering of 'utrumq; Testamentum'.
stance: own view (refutation of a quoted claim)

ref: Savonarola, Triumphus crucis, Liber IV, cap. VII (Latin, Bibliander 1550; pages 3 of the Paderborn excerpt, lines 'Nil praeterea diuinum' to 'Deo sacrificium'). English: Procter 1901, Book IV, ch. VII.
quote_orig: Nil præterea diuinum aut mirabile in hac secta, propter quod à Deo existimãda sit, apparet. Nullis enim, quemadmodum Christiana religio, fulcitur miraculis. Quod ipse Mahumetes attestatur: qui ait, Christo miraculorum uirtutem, quibus potissimè mundũ conuerteret, sibi uerò gladij potestatem esse cõcessam, & ad hoc missum ut per vim ad fidem suam populos cõpellat, perinde ac per tyrannidẽ uoluptatesq; fiat acceptabile Deo sacrificiũ.
quote_en: Among the Mahometans, again, we do not, as in the Christian religion, meet with any miracles, or manifestation of Divine phenomena. Mahomet, while acknowledging Christ as the messenger of God, commissioned to convert the world by miracles, said that he himself had been sent by Heaven to convert it by the sword.
keys: Nullis enim, quemadmodum Christiana religio, fulcitur miraculis
sibi uerò gladij potestatem esse cõcessam
what_it_says: Savonarola says the sect has nothing divine or wonderful that would show it to be from God, and no miracles as Christianity has; Muhammad himself said Christ was given the power of miracles to convert the world, while he himself was given the power of the sword.
context: Savonarola's argument that Islam lacks the miracles which authenticate the Christian religion; he uses Muhammad's own words (as he reports them) to show the contrast. The Latin is the Bibliander reprint; the English is Procter's rendering of the Italian.
limits: The 'Mahumetes attestatur' claim is Savonarola's report of a Qur'anic statement; the Qur'an passage is not checked here (UNVERIFIED as to the wording). Latin 'existimãda' and 'cõcessam' keep the printed tilde abbreviations.
stance: reporting (of Muhammad's claim) and own view

famous_note: As sav_01. The first sentence (Islam between Jews and heretics) is the opening of the chapter in both Latin and English.
ref: Savonarola, Triumphus crucis, Liber IV, cap. VII (Latin, Bibliander 1550; page 2 of the Paderborn excerpt, opening lines of the chapter). English: Procter 1901, Book IV, ch. VII.
quote_orig: Mahumetani quodammodo inter Iudaeos & Haereticos medij, postremo nobis loco convincendi superfuerunt. Nam & Iudaeorum circumcisionem imitantur, & omnium fere haereticorum errores coaceruarunt. Ideo non multo labore haec contra illos pugna conficitur.
quote_en: Mahometans, who observe the Jewish rite of circumcision and maintain almost every heretical doctrine, stand midway between Jews and heretics. It shall be our last, and not very difficult, task to refute them.
keys: non multo labore haec contra illos pugna conficitur
what_it_says: Savonarola places Muslims midway between Jews and heretics, because they keep Jewish circumcision and have adopted almost all heretical errors; he says they are the last group to be refuted and that this will not be hard.
context: This is the chapter's opening, setting the Muslims as the last of the adversaries in Book IV (after Jews and heretics). The Latin is the Bibliander reprint; the English is Procter's rendering of the Italian.
limits: Harshness is moderate: the sentence describes Islam as heretical and derivative of Judaism and heresy, without a direct insult. The Latin heading 'Mahumetanorum sectam omni ratione carere' is the chapter's title in the Bibliander reprint (Procter's chapter heading is different: 'The Utter Irrationality of the Mahometan Religion').

ref: Savonarola, Triumphus crucis, Liber IV, cap. VII (Latin, Bibliander 1550; page 3 of the Paderborn excerpt, lower part). English: Procter 1901, Book IV, ch. VII.
quote_orig: Quod autem maximũ inter eos habetur, est, ubi pronunciatur, Non est Deus nisi Deus, & Mahumetes nuncius eius. Et sæpe repetit Alcoranus, Deus est magnus, & potens: & notissima quædam de Deo, multis postea deturpata fabulis. Quas nec pueri nostri dignarentur.
quote_en: There is nothing striking in the doctrine contained in the Koran; yet the Mahometans think that they are uttering a wonderful saying, when they pronounce the words, “There is but one God, and Mahomet is His prophet”; “God is great and powerful”. This, and similar phrases, are often repeated, and to them are added fables, which our very children would ridicule.
keys: Non est Deus nisi Deus, & Mahumetes nuncius eius
what_it_says: Savonarola says the Muslims' central formula ('There is no god but God, and Muhammad is his messenger') is what they regard as the greatest matter; he says the Qur'an repeats that God is great and powerful, and adds fables about God that even children would not accept.
context: Savonarola's summary of the Islamic creed as he understood it, followed by his judgement that the doctrine has nothing striking in it. The Latin is the Bibliander reprint; the English is Procter's rendering of the Italian.
limits: Savonarola paraphrases the shahada (the Islamic profession of faith) as 'Non est Deus nisi Deus, & Mahumetes nuncius eius', which is a summary rather than the Arabic formula; the Qur'anic phrases 'Deus est magnus, & potens' are not checked. Procter's English puts the creed in quotation marks as a translation of the Italian.
stance: reporting (of Muslim formula) and own view

famous_note: Not verified as cited: I found no citation of this passage in the sources I read.
ref: Marsilius Ficinus, De christiana religione (1518 print), Caput XXXVI (running head; the printed page is XXXVI / folio XCIIII, PDF p. 185): Muhammad's denial of miracles and of divinity, and the Qur'anic claim that his teaching is for all righteous believers.
quote_orig: Multu.n. sua arrogantia temperauit cum dixit in alcorano: se miracula neq; fecisse: neq; facturum: plurima ignorare: esse purum hominem: quis nũciũ a deo inspiratũ: neq; se dare posse uenia peccatorũ. Voluit se inuocari: & adorari: confessus est insuper esse in libris suis nonnulla: de quoq; veritate dubitari possit. Ex quo apparet ipsum veritatis spiritum non fuisse: multum quoq; alcorani auctoritati detraxit.
own_translation_en: Muhammad's arrogance was in some measure tempered when he said in the Qur'an that he had neither performed miracles nor would perform them, that he knew many things not, that he was a pure man who had been inspired by God as a messenger, and that he could not give forgiveness of sins. He wanted himself to be invoked and adored; he admitted in his books that there were some things whose truth could be doubted. From this it appears that he did not have the spirit of truth, and he greatly detracted from the authority of the Qur'an. (Team's literal translation.)
licence_note: PDF of the 1518 print from archive.org (metadata: public domain mark 1.0). No public-domain English translation found; the 2022 Toronto translation is in copyright and was not read or quoted.
what_it_says: Ficino says Muhammad, in the Qur'an, denied performing miracles, called himself a mere man, and admitted that some things in his books might be doubted; therefore he did not have the spirit of truth and weakened the Qur'an's authority.
context: Ficino's chapter on the Muslim view of Christ and Muhammad (Caput XXXVI); he argues that Muhammad's own admissions about miracles and his book destroy his claim to authority. The Latin is from the 1518 print; the passage is a brief aside within a larger apology for Christianity.
limits: Latin transcribed by visual reading of the 1518 page image (PDF p. 185); the scan is clear, but a few words (e.g. 'nũciũ', 'de quoq;', 'purum hominem') are uncertain and abbreviation marks are normalised. Ficino's account of the Qur'an is not checked against the Qur'anic text (UNVERIFIED). quote_en is «» (no public-domain English).
stance: own view (Ficino's critique of the Qur'an's author)

ref: Marsilius Ficinus, De christiana religione (1518 print), Caput XXXVII ('Causa erroris Iudeorum Maumethensium gentilium'), printed page XXXVII / XCV (PDF p. 186-187).
quote_orig: Violenta maumethis regis arabum manus: septemq; regum ipsi ex eius familia per ordinem succedentium leges: Accessit & licentia largior: uerũ quid gentiles olim a uera hebreorum religione detorsit: mandata ambitiosorum principũ: etas parum erudita: profusa licentia: fallacia demonum malignorum.
own_translation_en: The violent hand of Muhammad, king of the Arabs, and the laws of seven kings of his family succeeding one another in order: to this was added a greater licence. But what turned the gentiles of old away from the true religion of the Hebrews was the commands of ambitious princes, an unlearned age, unrestrained licence, and the deceit of malignant demons. (Team's literal translation.)
what_it_says: Ficino attributes the spread of Muhammad's religion to the violent hand of the Arab king Muhammad and his successors, and to a licence and deceit which he compares with the gentile error that turned men away from the Hebrew religion.
context: Ficino's historical explanation for the origin of Islam (and of the errors of Jews and gentiles) in Caput XXXVII; he describes Islam as an error of the same kind as the pagan errors, produced by demons, and says Christians alone have a religion free from error. The passage is part of a broader argument on the causes of error.
limits: The 'violent hand' phrase is a rhetorical charge rather than a claim about specific events; Ficino gives no sources here. The Latin 'leges:' punctuation and 'uerũ quid' are read from the image and may vary slightly. Ficino's 'demons' explanation is his theological framing, not a historical claim. quote_en is «».

ref: Marsilius Ficinus, De christiana religione (1518 print), Caput XXXVI (running head truncated in the scan; folio not read; PDF p. 184): the Qur'anic 'two gods' and Trinity accusation.
quote_orig: Atq; hinc in alcorano binarium deorum numerum detestatur: quod etiam a christianis est alienum: deum unum patrem filium spiritumq; putantibus. Preterea: quoties incidit in trinitatis nomen: hõ tante rei prorsus ignarus: christianos falso nimium: & inepte calumniatur: qd tres deos adorent: nesciens proprietates diuinarum distinguere personarum: ac simul seruare diuine substantie unitatem.
own_translation_en: And from this he (Muhammad) denounces in the Qur'an the number of two gods, which is also alien to Christians, who hold that God is one, Father, Son and Spirit. Moreover, whenever he touches on the name of the Trinity, a man entirely ignorant of so great a matter, he falsely and foolishly accuses Christians of worshipping three gods, not knowing how to distinguish the properties of the divine persons and at the same time keep the unity of the divine substance. (Team's literal translation.)
what_it_says: Ficino says Muhammad rejects a 'two-god' idea in the Qur'an that Christians also reject, and wrongly accuses Christians of worshipping three gods, because he does not understand the distinction of persons within the one divine substance.
context: Part of Ficino's discussion (Caput XXXVI) of Muhammad's misunderstanding of Christian mysteries; he argues that Muhammad, while speaking of God's breath, spirit and word, nonetheless affirms the Christian doctrine that Christ was God's Son born of a virgin.
limits: The passage describes Muhammad's denunciation of Trinitarian belief as Ficino reads it; the Qur'anic text is not checked against this reading (UNVERIFIED). Latin read from PDF p. 184 image; the running head is truncated in the scan. 'hõ', 'qd', 'nesciens' are printed abbreviations or read forms; flagged. quote_en is «».

ref: Marsilius Ficinus, De christiana religione (1518 print), Caput XII ('Christi auctoritas apud Maumethenses'), printed page XXIIII (PDF p. 47), with the earlier sentence on p. 46.
quote_orig: Alter maumethis error: & quidem manifestior est: quòd quando satellites illi sacerdotum: qui coniicere manus in iesum conabatur: ceciderunt: deus ut maumethes putat: repente: & clam iesum in cœlum rapuit. Illi cum surrexissent: alium quendam iesu similem comprehendentes uerberauerunt: & cruci affixerunt: hoc a manicheis accepisse uidetur.
own_translation_en: The second error of Muhammad is more manifest: when those henchmen of the priests who tried to lay hands on Jesus fell down, God, as Muhammad thinks, suddenly and secretly carried Jesus up into heaven. When they rose again, they seized another man like Jesus, beat him, and crucified him; this he seems to have taken from the Manichaeans. (Team's literal translation.)
keys: alium quendam iesu similem comprehendentes uerberauerunt
what_it_says: Ficino reports the Qur'anic account in which Jesus was taken up to God and another man was crucified in his place, and he says Muhammad took this from the Manichaeans.
context: From Ficino's chapter on Muhammad's view of Christ (Caput XII): he lists two errors of Muhammad, the first about Christ's divinity and the second about the crucifixion. The second error is called 'more manifest'. The passage precedes Ficino's conclusion that Christianity is the most excellent of all religions (see fic_07).
limits: Ficino's account of the Qur'anic substitution story is not checked against the Qur'an (UNVERIFIED as to content). His attribution to the Manichaeans is his own historical claim and is not checked. Latin read from PDF p. 47 image; 'repente' is printed with a nasal stroke, normalised here. quote_en is «».
stance: own view (Ficino's critique of a quoted narrative)

ref: Marsilius Ficinus, De christiana religione (1518 print), Caput XXXVII (heading on PDF p. 186; the passage continues to p. 186): Muslim beliefs about the Testaments, Christ, the Antichrist and the 'Lord's Prayer'.
quote_orig: Vnde et maumethis sectatores: eo concedente: fatentur: nouo testamento accedente: ueteris testamenti ritus magna ex parte merito cessasse. Testamentum uetus nouumq; eo pacto intelligunt: & obseruant: quo expositi: madauitq; maumethes: qui se utriusq; uerissimum interpretem esse asseuerauit: creationem mundi: ade progeniem: historiam omnem hebraicam probant: & christi doctrinam. Expectant antichristum fore pessimum hominem: quem a christo occisum iri putant. Item corporum resurrectionem: ultimum iudicium: supplicia & premia sempiterna: christum proximum deo sedentem collocant Maumethenses christi oratione: qua & nos quotidiana: utuntur ad deum: pater noster: & reliqua. Sed ubi nos dicimus: & ne nos inducas: ipsi dicunt: deus fuit & deus erit: maumethes missus a deo.
own_translation_en: And so the followers of Muhammad, with his consent, confess that with the addition of the New Testament the rites of the Old Testament have in large part rightly ceased. They understand and keep both Testaments in the way that Muhammad, who declared himself the most true interpreter of both, set out and commanded: they confirm the creation of the world, the lineage of Adam, all the Hebrew history, and the teaching of Christ. They expect the Antichrist to be the worst man, whom they believe was killed by Christ. Likewise they hold the resurrection of bodies, the last judgment, eternal punishments and rewards; they place Christ, sitting next to God, and the Muhammadans use the prayer of Christ, which we also say daily, 'Our Father' and the rest. But where we say 'and lead us not', they say: 'God was, and God will be; Muhammad sent from God.' (Team's literal translation.)
keys: Sed ubi nos dicimus: & ne nos inducas: ipsi dicunt
deus fuit & deus erit: maumethes missus a deo
what_it_says: Ficino describes what Muslims, in his account, believe about the two Testaments, Christ, the Antichrist and the resurrection, and says they recite the Lord's Prayer but alter its end, replacing 'lead us not into temptation' with a formula about God and Muhammad.
context: Ficino's chapter on the causes of error, where he sets out the Muslim position against Jews and gentiles; the passage is descriptive, with an ironic close. It is part of a longer argument that Muslims and Jews misread Scripture.
limits: The description of Muslim belief is Ficino's account and is not checked against Islamic sources (UNVERIFIED). The final 'altered Lord's Prayer' claim is a polemical report, probably drawn from a Christian source; no source is given. The final phrase is read as 'deus fuit & deus erit' from the scan (the word 'erit' is partly abbreviated). quote_en is «».
stance: reporting (of Muslim belief) and own view

ref: Marsilius Ficinus, De christiana religione (1518 print), Caput XII, printed page XXIIII (PDF p. 47): conclusion that Christian law is the most excellent of all sects.
quote_orig: Concludere possumus xpianam legem apud oes sectas gentilium: iudeorum: maumethensium: re uera omnium excellentissimam esse concedi. Quisq; enim istorum: quauis affectione quadam nature: consuetudinisq;: uel fictitiis proprie heresim ceteris preferat: christiana tamen: excepta sua: reliquis anteponit.
own_translation_en: We can conclude that the Christian law is conceded, in truth, to be the most excellent of all, among the sects of the gentiles, of the Jews and of the Muhammadans. For each of them, though by some affection of nature, custom, or fictitious devices of his own he may prefer his own heresy to the others, yet puts Christian law above the rest, except his own. (Team's literal translation.)
keys: maumethensium: re uera omnium excellentissimam esse concedi
christiana tamen: excepta sua: reliquis anteponit
what_it_says: Ficino concludes that the Christian law is by common concession the most excellent of all sects (pagan, Jewish, Muslim), because even adherents of other sects tend to rank Christianity above the rest, apart from their own.
context: Ficino's conclusion to the section on Muhammad's view of Christ (Caput XII). It is an argument for Christian excellence from comparison, not a doctrinal attack on Islam.
limits: Harshness low (1): the passage is comparative and not an attack. The Latin abbreviation 'xpianam' (Christianam) is printed with the Christ abbreviation and is normalised here. The claim that adherents prefer Christianity is Ficino's argument, not an observed fact. quote_en is «».

ref: Marsilius Ficinus, De christiana religione (1518 print), Caput XII ('Christi auctoritas apud Maumethenses'), printed page XXIII (PDF p. 45): opening of the chapter.
quote_orig: Maumethenses christiani quodamodo esse uidetur: quauis heretici arrianorum; manicheorumq; sectatores: confitetur certe rex eorum maumethes: iesum xpm dei uirtute: sapientiam [aiam?]: flatu: spiritu; uerboq; afflatu quodam diuino: ex maria uirgine perpetua natum: suscitasse mortuos alia miracula plurima p ceteris diuinitus effecisse.
own_translation_en: The Muhammadans seem in a way to be Christians, although they are heretics, followers of the Arians and the Manichaeans: their king Muhammad certainly confesses that Jesus, by the power of God, wisdom, (uncertain word), breath, spirit and word, born of the Virgin Mary, and that he raised the dead and performed many other miracles beyond the others, divinely. (Team's literal translation; the uncertain word is unresolved.)
what_it_says: Ficino says the Muhammadans seem in some way Christian, although they follow heretical Arian or Manichaean lines, and that their king Muhammad confesses Jesus to be great by God's power. (The rest of the sentence, which in the scan continues with Jesus's birth from the Virgin and his miracles, was read but is not transcribed here.)
context: The opening of Ficino's chapter on Christ's authority among the Muhammadans (Caput XII): he begins with what Muhammad concedes about Christ, before attacking Muhammad's two main errors (fic_04).
limits: The word in brackets ('aiam', printed with a tilde-type abbreviation; read as 'animam' or similar) is uncertain and is marked [aiam?] rather than resolved. The attribution 'quauis heretici arrianorum; manicheorumq;' is Ficino's. The 'Muhammad confesses' claim is Ficino's reading of the Qur'an, not checked here. Own translation is provisional for the untranscribed part. quote_en is «».
stance: reporting (of Muhammad's words, as Ficino gives them)
